lessons.title: How a name becomes an address: nsswitch, hosts, resolv.conf
lessons.goal:
Learn the path a program takes to turn `example.com` into an IP address, and which files control it.

Why it matters: "it works with the IP but not the name" is a DNS question. You must know which layer to blame: the program, the C library, the local files or the DNS server.

setup.note: Steps with sudo edit /etc/hosts for a moment (a copy is restored at the end) and run a tiny DNS server on 127.0.0.1:5353. Use a throwaway machine. Needs dig (`bind-utils`) and tcpdump.

steps.title: Programs ask the C library
steps.text: A program calls `getaddrinfo()` in libc. libc reads `/etc/nsswitch.conf` to learn **where** to look and in what order. The `hosts:` line lists the sources: `files` (/etc/hosts), `dns`, `myhostname` and so on.

steps.title: getent asks the same way a program does
steps.text: `getent hosts NAME` goes through libc and nsswitch, exactly like `ping` or `curl`. Names with no answer give exit code 2.

steps.title: /etc/hosts: a local override
steps.text: Because `files` comes first, an entry in `/etc/hosts` wins over DNS. We add a fake name, ask libc, and remove it again.

run.cmd: echo '10.200.7.7 labhost.example' | sudo tee -a /etc/hosts > /dev/null; getent hosts labhost.example | tr -s ' ' ' '
sudo sed -i '/labhost.example/d' /etc/hosts; getent hosts labhost.example; echo "exit code after removal: $?"

steps.title: /etc/resolv.conf: which DNS servers
steps.text: For the `dns` source libc reads `/etc/resolv.conf`: the `nameserver` lines (up to three), a `search` list of domains tried for short names, and options (`timeout`, `attempts`). NetworkManager or systemd-resolved usually generates it.

run.output: ; Any changes made to this file will be

steps.under: The resolver sends the query to the first nameserver and waits `timeout` seconds (default 5) before trying the next one, and repeats `attempts` times (default 2). A dead first nameserver therefore adds 5 seconds to every lookup: a classic cause of "everything is slow".

steps.title: dig talks DNS directly and ignores /etc/hosts
steps.text: `dig` is a DNS client: it sends a query to a DNS server and shows the answer. It does **not** use nsswitch, so it does not see `/etc/hosts`. This difference is a favourite troubleshooting trap.

run.cmd: echo '10.200.7.7 labhost.example' | sudo tee -a /etc/hosts > /dev/null; getent hosts labhost.example | wc -l | awk '{print "getent finds it:", $1}'; dig +short labhost.example | wc -l | awk '{print "dig finds it:", $1}'; sudo sed -i '/labhost.example/d' /etc/hosts
run.output:
getent finds it: 1
dig finds it: 0

quiz.q: Which file decides the order of name sources (files, dns)?
`ping name` works with the entry in /etc/hosts, but `dig name` shows nothing. Why?
options: dig queries DNS servers and does not read /etc/hosts
The same libc path as normal programs

quiz.q: A dead first nameserver in resolv.conf causes...
options: Several seconds of delay on lookups before the next server is tried

check.scenario: Users say a website opens only after 5 seconds, every time. Pinging the IP is instant. What is the most likely cause and how do you confirm it?
check.answer: A slow or dead **first nameserver** in `/etc/resolv.conf` (5 s timeout) or an IPv6 (AAAA) lookup issue. Confirm with `time getent hosts name` and `dig @FIRST_NS name` versus `dig @SECOND_NS name`; with `strace -f -e trace=network,connect getent hosts name` you can see the timeouts. Fix by removing the dead server or reducing `timeout`.

lessons.title: dig and the DNS protocol, with a tiny DNS server
lessons.goal:
Read a DNS answer in full, see the query and reply as real packets, and meet the response codes, using a DNS server we write ourselves.

Why it matters: DNS is behind almost every outage story. You should be able to read `dig` output and tell NXDOMAIN from NODATA from a timeout.

setup.note: Steps with sudo edit /etc/hosts for a moment (a copy is restored at the end) and run a tiny DNS server on 127.0.0.1:5353. Use a throwaway machine. Needs dig (`bind-utils`) and tcpdump.

steps.title: A DNS server in 30 lines
steps.text: DNS queries are small UDP packets. This Python program answers type **A** queries for two names and says "no such name" (NXDOMAIN) for anything else. It listens on 127.0.0.1 port 5353. Save it as `dnsd.py`.

code.src:
import socket, struct

ANSWERS = {"lab.example.": "10.200.8.8", "www.lab.example.": "10.200.8.9"}


def parse_name(data, pos):
    labels = []
    while data[pos]:
        n = data[pos]
        labels.append(data[pos + 1:pos + 1 + n].decode())
        pos += n + 1
    return ".".join(labels) + ".", pos + 1


sock = socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_DGRAM)
sock.bind(("127.0.0.1", 5353))
while True:
    data, client = sock.recvfrom(512)
    name, end = parse_name(data, 12)
    qtype, qclass = struct.unpack("!HH", data[end:end + 4])
    question = data[12:end + 4]
    ip = ANSWERS.get(name.lower())
    flags = 0x8180 if ip else 0x8183                    # response + recursion available; or NXDOMAIN
    answers = 1 if ip and qtype == 1 else 0             # only type A (1) gets an answer
    reply = data[:2] + struct.pack("!HHHHH", flags, 1, answers, 0, 0) + question
    if answers:
        reply += b"\xc0\x0c" + struct.pack("!HHIH", 1, 1, 60, 4) + socket.inet_aton(ip)
    sock.sendto(reply, client)

run.cmd: python3 dnsd.py > /dev/null 2>&1 & echo $! > dns.pid; sleep 0.5; echo started

steps.title: Ask it with dig
steps.text: `dig @SERVER -p PORT NAME` sends one query to that server. `+noall +comments +question +answer` prints the header, the question and the answer section only.

run.output:
;; Got answer:
;; ->>HEADER<<- opcode: QUERY, status: NOERROR, id: 29575
;; flags: qr rd ra; QUERY: 1, ANSWER: 1, AUTHORITY: 0, ADDITIONAL: 0
;; QUESTION SECTION:
;lab.example.			IN	A
;; ANSWER SECTION:
lab.example.		60	IN	A	10.200.8.8

steps.after: `status: NOERROR` is success. `flags: qr rd ra` mean: this is a response, recursion was desired, recursion is available. The answer line has the name, the **TTL** (60 seconds: how long a resolver may cache it), class `IN`, type `A` and the data.

steps.title: Short output, and the other cases
steps.text:
`+short` prints only the data. Three outcomes you must tell apart:

- **NOERROR with an answer**: the name exists and has that type.
- **NXDOMAIN**: the name does not exist.
- **NOERROR with no answer (NODATA)**: the name exists but has no record of that type (here: no AAAA).

run.cmd: dig @127.0.0.1 -p 5353 lab.example AAAA +noall +comments | grep -oE 'status: [A-Z]+|ANSWER: [0-9]+' | tr '\n' ' '; echo

steps.title: The packets on the wire
steps.text: We capture the exchange on loopback. tcpdump decodes UDP port 5353 as multicast DNS, so the query is printed as `A (QM)? lab.example.` (the standard port 53 would print `A? lab.example.`). The reply carries one answer, `1/0/0` (answers/authority/additional). The first number is the query ID that matches request and reply.

run.cmd: sudo timeout 3 tcpdump -i lo -nn -l udp port 5353 -c 2 2>/dev/null | sed -E 's/^[0-9:.]+ IP //; s/127.0.0.1\.[0-9]{5}/CLIENT/; s/^CLIENT > 127.0.0.1.5353: [0-9]+/CLIENT > SERVER: id/; s/^127.0.0.1.5353 > CLIENT: [0-9]+/SERVER > CLIENT: id/' > dns.cap & T=$!; sleep 1; dig @127.0.0.1 -p 5353 lab.example +short > /dev/null; wait $T; cat dns.cap
run.output:
[2] 3480104
CLIENT > SERVER: id+ [1au] A (QM)? lab.example. (52)
SERVER > CLIENT: id 1/0/0 A 10.200.8.8 (45)

steps.under: DNS uses UDP port 53 for small messages (up to 512 bytes, or about 1232 with EDNS0) and falls back to **TCP** when a reply is truncated (the `tc` flag) or for zone transfers. DNSSEC and large answers make TCP more common. A firewall that blocks 53/tcp causes odd failures only for big answers.

steps.title: Record types you meet
steps.text:
- **A** / **AAAA**: IPv4 / IPv6 address.
- **CNAME**: an alias to another name.
- **MX**: mail servers. **TXT**: text (SPF, verification).
- **NS**: the servers responsible for a zone. **SOA**: zone parameters.
- **PTR**: reverse lookup (address to name).

A **resolver** (recursive) walks from the root to the authoritative server for you and caches the answer for its TTL. A **stub** resolver (libc) only asks one such server.

options: The name exists with no record of that type

quiz.q: A reply with `status: NOERROR` and `ANSWER: 0` for an AAAA query means...
options: The name exists but has no AAAA record

quiz.q: What is the TTL in a DNS answer?
options: Time to live of the packet
How long the answer may be cached
quiz.explain: Seconds a resolver may cache the record.

options: For truncated replies, zone transfers and large answers

check.scenario: `dig +short www.example.com` returns nothing, but `dig www.example.com` with its full output shows `status: NOERROR` and `ANSWER: 0`. What does that tell you?
check.answer: The name exists but has no record of the type you asked for (A by default): it may have only AAAA or a CNAME to a name without A. Try `dig AAAA`, `dig ANY`/`CNAME`, and compare the authoritative server's answer (`dig @ns1... name`). NXDOMAIN would instead mean the name itself does not exist.

interview.q: How does a program resolve a hostname on Linux?
interview.a: It calls getaddrinfo() in libc, which follows /etc/nsswitch.conf (usually files, then dns), reads /etc/hosts and queries the nameservers in /etc/resolv.conf. See [the lesson](#/lesson/30/name-resolution).

interview.q: Why does dig not see an entry in /etc/hosts?
interview.a: dig is a DNS client and talks to a DNS server directly; it does not use nsswitch or /etc/hosts. Use `getent hosts` to test what programs see.

interview.q: What is the difference between NXDOMAIN and NODATA?
interview.a: NXDOMAIN: the name does not exist. NODATA: the name exists, but has no record of the requested type (NOERROR with zero answers). See [the lesson](#/lesson/30/dig-and-dns-protocol).

interview.q: What is a TTL and what happens when it is long?
interview.a: Cache lifetime of a record. A long TTL means fewer queries but slow propagation of changes; lower it before a planned migration.
A, AAAA, CNAME, MX, TXT, NS, SOA, PTR, SRV, CAA.

interview.q: Why is every lookup 5 seconds slow?
interview.a: The first nameserver in resolv.conf is unreachable (timeout 5 s) before the second is used, or an AAAA query is blocked. Check with `time getent hosts` and `dig @server`.

glossary.def: The Domain Name System: a distributed database that maps names to addresses and other data.
The file that tells libc the order of sources for names, users and more.
The file listing DNS servers and search domains for the libc resolver.
Time to live: seconds a DNS record may be cached.
DNS response: the name does not exist.
Software that looks up names, often with a cache (recursive) or as a stub in libc.
A DNS server that holds the real data for a zone.
